rss_0_1790027444.title: Chemist-aligned retrosynthesis by ensembling diverse inductive bias models
rss_0_1790027444.text: Chemical synthesis remains a critical bottleneck in the discovery and manufacture of functional small molecules1−3. While AI-assisted synthesis planning has proliferated in recent years, a detailed understanding of its failure modes has not been achieved, and models still struggle with predicting less frequent, yet strategically critical reactions, as well as hallucinated, incorrect predictions misaligned with chemists’ expectations4−12. In this work, we analyze the failure modes of current AI models and propose RetroChimera: a frontier retrosynthesis model, built upon two newly developed components with complementary inductive biases, integrated via a novel, learning-based ensembling strategy. Through experiments across several orders of magnitude in data scale, we show RetroChimera outperforms leading baselines, demonstrating robustness outside the training data, as well as the ability to learn from very small numbers of examples per reaction class. Using both pairwise and pointwise setups, we find that organic chemists prefer predictions from RetroChimera over published reference reactions and over other AI models. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer and fine-tuning on internal datasets from two major pharmaceutical companies, showing robust generalization under distribution shift. Our work demonstrates the viability of deep learning for accurate synthesis prediction in increasingly challenging regimes.

rss_1_1790027446.title: Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities
rss_1_1790027446.text:
The university I lead is more than four centuries old and has seen political orders rise and fall. I have not, but I work each day in an institution that remembers those changes — in its archives, statutes and culture of argument. The conditions that make knowledge trustworthy, such as independent peer review, openness about methods and data and the ability to correct earlier work, are changing in ways that reach the core of what a university is for.

How universities came to be — and why they are in trouble now

Those conditions are under pressure in a growing number of countries, and the familiar tools of quiet diplomacy, internal negotiation and isolated warnings no longer keep up with the pace of change. For example, in the past decade, governments in various countries have narrowed the space for independent evidence in different ways.

In the United States, changes to research-funding mechanisms and programme priorities in areas such as climate science and gender research, and the sidelining of environmental and public-health expertise, have shown how quickly political decisions can affect the systems that produce independent evidence (see go.nature.com/4hgg3ym and go.nature.com/4zzmtur). European academies have voiced their concerns in public statements on the pressures facing US science and international collaboration1–2 (see also go.nature.com/4a3pn9s).

In Hungary, a sustained legal campaign around foreign higher-education institutions drove Budapest’s Central European University out of the country to Vienna in 2019. In 2020, the Court of Justice of the European Union found those legal changes incompatible with EU law4,5. The political landscape in Hungary has shifted since then, but the legal tools used and the damage to institutional autonomy and academic freedom remain instructive.

Elsewhere, grant language is being rewritten to steer funding priorities towards favoured themes such as economic competitiveness, innovation and national security. Access to public data in sensitive areas such as climate and health is being reduced, and researchers are adapting proposals accordingly, sometimes by avoiding or adding certain topics or terms to maximize their chances in the next funding round.

The details differ, yet the pattern is familiar to many of us who work in universities. One question keeps returning: when governments or funders intervene in universities, do they strengthen or weaken the checks that make knowledge trustworthy?

Others have warned about these threats to independent enquiry already1,2,6. Here, I try to turn these concerns into a set of principles that can guide real decisions in the messy situations academics face. They can be used as a test for any measure that affects universities, and apply to governments, funders and university leaders alike.

They are written for people who have to decide, often under time pressure, where legitimate steering of a publicly funded system ends and interference with independent knowledge begins. They concern both the freedom of academics to pursue questions wherever the evidence leads, and the ability of universities to protect that work from undue influence. These are distinct but connected responsibilities, because pressures on one often weaken the other.

The first three principles set out why independent enquiry must be protected and how that protection is anchored in the university’s core task. The last three show when that protection has to be weighed against other legitimate concerns.

Ground academic freedom in the duty to produce reliable knowledge

Universities have a responsibility to produce reliable knowledge of lasting public value — including for people who will never set foot in a lecture hall — and to teach students how to think using that knowledge. Academic freedom is the working condition that makes this possible.

I learnt this from supervisors who allowed me to ask awkward questions and from students who pushed back in seminars. We are answerable first for the quality and integrity of the knowledge we produce and teach. Academic freedom is one of the tools that allow us to live up to that responsibility.

Discussions about academic freedom often start with rights and only later bring in responsibility as a limit. I prefer to reverse that order: universities are first accountable for the quality of the knowledge they create and pass on, and academic freedom and institutional autonomy are the conditions in which to do this well.

Research that bends towards political or commercial pressure carries that pressure into the questions that are asked, the methods that are chosen and the outcomes that are presented7,8. Teaching that pushes political instructions to the fore trains students to adapt their thinking to approved answers instead of testing arguments against disciplinary standards (see go.nature.com/4a3pn9s).

Teaching students how to use reliable knowledge to inform their thinking is a university’s core task.Credit: AzmanJaka/Getty

External directives that decide in advance which questions might be asked or which answers are acceptable reduce the space to question assumptions and to correct mistakes. When the people who produce and teach knowledge cannot work independently, they gradually lose the ability to correct each other and to correct those in power.

Quality is often the main reason given for defending academic freedom. It is also the main language used to justify limiting it. Some governments frame measures that reduce universities’ capacity for independent enquiry in terms of quality, integrity, balance or public safety, presenting these interventions as ways to protect academic standards. What matters is how knowledge is produced in practice, whether others can see and test what has been done and whether it proves reliable over decades.

Measures that genuinely improve knowledge make methods and results easier to check and to challenge. However, changing grant calls to favour certain answers, screening researchers for their views or taking uncomfortable data offline weakens that scrutiny and minimizes what can be known from work that has already been done. The test for any such measure is whether it strengthens independent scrutiny, and with it the university’s ability to meet its responsibility to society.

Protect questions that have value that cannot be shown in advance

Curiosity-driven research often leads to applications that no one can predict. If researchers limit in advance which questions they will pursue, they also limit the futures that science can open up.

There are various examples of such applications that were initially unpredictable. Work on how bacteria defend themselves against viruses became CRISPR gene editing, now the basis of a therapy for sickle-cell disease. Research in linguistics and digital humanities helped to build translation tools and search systems. Long-term epidemiological cohort studies underpin public-health guidance on smoking, diet, workplace safety and environmental exposure. Decades of work on messenger RNA and lipid-nanoparticle delivery became the platform for COVID-19 vaccines when the world needed them. None of these lines of work would have scored highly for societal relevance at the start.

Key US science panels are being axed — and others are becoming less open

Research should speak to societal challenges, but funding systems also need to preserve room for questions with a value that cannot yet be specified. Narrowly defined relevance criteria tend to reward safe, incremental projects and push researchers towards low-risk enquiry. Free enquiry matters precisely because scientists do not know in advance which questions will turn out to be important.

A government that wants to base policy on robust knowledge depends on a research system that can generate and test that knowledge independently. Cutting public investment in fundamental research might reduce spending today, but it shifts the cost into the future — through missed treatments, weaker prevention, lost innovation and a reduced capacity to respond when the next crisis arrives. The test is whether a measure unduly narrows the range of questions that can still be asked.

Treat universities as democratic infrastructure

Universities disperse power in practice by training professionals who can question official decisions, by producing analyses that can contradict government or corporate claims and by placing independent expertise inside courts of law, in the media and in public debate. Together with the executive, legislative and judicial branches, and with a free press and civil society, universities form a pillar of a society that is built on democracy, human rights and the rule of law. When that wider structure is weakened, universities are usually affected as well.

Hungary shows how this can unfold. Between 2017 and 2019, Viktor Orbán’s government reduced the independence of universities and research institutes by transferring control of research funding from the national academy of sciences to a new research network. The network’s board is chaired by a government-appointed minister’s nominee. The government used higher-education law to force the Central European University abroad, and brought law courts, the press and civil society under tighter political control through parallel legislative changes4.

Elsewhere, earmarked funding, new laws on cooperation, politicized appointments to governing boards and a steady public attack on expertise point in a similar direction. Examples of such trends are described in global and EU-wide academic freedom monitors and national reports9–11.

It does not take dramatic events abroad to damage academic freedom. In my own country, the Netherlands, the national academy warned in 2025 that large budget cuts increase the pressure to shift from independent to commissioned research, and that a proposed screening law on knowledge security would limit researchers’ freedom to choose their collaboration partners. It also documented self-censorship after researchers were intimidated in public debates12. Rectors of Dutch universities warned in the same year of a growing political tendency to steer the content of scientific debate and teaching (see go.nature.com/3v3ktjj).

Institutional autonomy means being accountable to the public for the quality and integrity of knowledge, rather than to a government for whether it finds the conclusions politically acceptable. Rules and accountability frameworks are not in themselves a problem. Many exist to protect people, ensure workplace safety or guard public funds. A problem arises when their combined effect, including funding conditions, reporting requirements and rules on cooperation, shifts the centre of control from the university to the ministry. One form of accountability strengthens independent knowledge; the other replaces it with political acceptability.

Hold security and openness as a single responsibility

The case for academic freedom is linked to that for research security. The risks of espionage, loss of intellectual property and harmful use of sensitive knowledge are real, and universities cannot ignore them.

At the same time, security measures that are designed without attention to academic freedom can unintentionally narrow independent enquiry and place a great deal of control in the hands of those who manage access to data, infrastructure and international collaboration.

rss_2_1790027447.title: Losing your way of life to climate change matters — and we need a way to measure it
rss_2_1790027447.text:
Salt harvesters in Gujarat, India, often have to work through extreme heatwaves.

The first time I began to understand climate loss as a mental-health issue was not while reading a report or attending a summit. It was while listening to people describe what they feared losing.

While working with coastal communities in Kenya, I heard concerns that initially sounded economic: declining fish catches, disrupted marine ecosystems and shrinking livelihoods. But the conversations quickly turned deeper. Community members spoke of mounting anxiety, growing substance use in unemployed young men and rises in gender-based violence, sex tourism and adolescent pregnancies as poverty intensified.

People also worried about the erosion of traditions tied to the sea: knowledge passed between generations; community rituals and identities rooted in fishing livelihoods. What they feared losing was not only income, but also stability, belonging and hope for the future.

The rise of eco-anxiety: scientists wake up to the mental-health toll of climate change

Over the years, as a clinical psychologist and public-health researcher, I have heard concerns about climate change that extend far beyond homes, crops and livelihoods. People speak about losing their sense of belonging. They worry that their children will grow up disconnected from the places that have defined their families for generations. They talk about grief for disappearing landscapes, anxiety about an uncertain future and the exhaustion that comes from living through repeated crises.

As governments prepare for a round of negotiations at COP31, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, in Antalya, Turkey, in November — and as I and others participate in Climate Week NYC 2026 in New York City this week — discussions about climate-related loss and damage are needed urgently. Communities are already experiencing irreversible harm: permanent displacement, destruction of ecosystems, loss of cultural heritage and repeated disasters that are eroding resilience. The devastating flood in Nepal last month is one glaring example.

Mental health sits at the centre of those losses, yet remains mostly invisible in the systems designed to address them. When climate policy acknowledges mental health, it is usually through adaptation, focusing on helping people to cope with ongoing changes. These policies can encompass preparedness, psychological first aid, resilience programmes and stronger health systems. Investments in these areas are essential, but they address only part of the problem.

Why environmental treaties must also address mental health

What happens when people cannot adapt? What happens when a fishing community can no longer sustain its way of life? People often experience climate change not as a single disaster, but as gradual erosion of health, livelihoods, social cohesion and dignity. I have seen this in female salt workers in the Indian state of Gujarat, where members of a grass-roots trade union struggle to work in rising temperatures — at times exceeding 50 °C — that compound physical hardship, economic insecurity and chronic stress.

The UN’s framework for climate loss and damage, one of the few areas in climate policy that recognizes harms that are not purely economic, offers an opportunity to redress these pressures. Mental health should not be treated as an afterthought. It should be recognized as a legitimate area in which governments should invest, harms should be measured and institutions should be held accountable in addressing these harms. But this raises an uncomfortable question: how do we place a value on mental health?

rss_3_1790027448.title: Edible batteries power medical devices in the body
rss_3_1790027448.text:
This ingestible capsule, tested in pigs, contains a biodegradable paper battery (large brown circular structure) and a radio-frequency identification (RFID) tag (black lines).Credit: Mehmet Say

A battery made with a substance resembling edible rice paper can power swallowable electronic medical devices. And after the battery has been safely digested, its broken-down ingredients can be absorbed by the body. The tiny power source has so far been tested in pigs, but the hope is that one day it could provide electricity for ingestible personalized devices that monitor human health or implanted ones that deliver electrical impulses to treat disease.

The researchers who built the battery tested it in two devices: one with a radio-frequency identification (RFID) tag that can transmit data from inside the body, and one that electrically stimulates the stomach to trigger the release of hunger-regulating hormones. Their findings are described today in the journal Nature Chemical Engineering1.

Ingredient overhaul

Conventional batteries can be dangerous, says Giovanni Traverso, a mechanical engineer at the Massachussetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge and a co-author of the study. If an ingested medical device breaks open and the battery inside it leaks, it can cause chemical burns. The battery can also release toxic materials as it passes through the digestive system. So Traverso wanted to build a battery entirely from non-toxic materials that would be absorbed by the body, making accidents unlikely.

“We were highly restricted in what materials to use,” Traverso says. Batteries normally contain electrodes for storing chemical energy, electrolytes that ferry charges between the electrodes and packaging to hold it all together. Lithium-ion and alkaline batteries often contain toxic metals, organic electrolytes that would accumulate in the body and plastic casings that can fragment into sharp pieces.

Rice paper, shown here drying on a bamboo lattice, was the inspiration for the coating on an edible battery.Credit: Mel Longhurst/VW Pics/Universal Images Group via Getty

Traverso’s group chose magnesium and molybdenum trioxide for their electrodes. Magnesium and molybdenum are metallic micronutrients that the body needs in small amounts, and when paired together in a battery, they provide a voltage high enough to power electronics. For an electrolyte, the researchers chose a biodegradable ionic liquid, instead of the poorly performing buffered saline used in some previous biocompatible battery designs.

Packaging was also key. The researchers needed a material that would support the other parts of the battery, without dampening overall performance by being electrically insulating. It also needed to have a large surface area and be made of a material the body can safely absorb when the device is no longer needed. “We were partly inspired by candies that have an edible rice-paper wrapper,” Traverso says. The cellulose-based coating they used for the battery dissolves over time, like those sweet wrappers. And the whole thing is dipped in beeswax to slow down the effects of stomach acid.

Open wide

The team tested the batteries in simulated gastric fluid, and found that they began coming apart within two weeks and completely dissolved after several months. Next, the researchers packaged the batteries together with other fully biodegradable, non-toxic electronics inside gel capsules, and tested them in pigs. An RFID-tracking device inside a swallowable gel capsule transmitted signals to a reader outside the pigs’ bodies. And an electrical stimulation device placed in pigs’ stomachs through endoscopy caused an increase in levels of the hunger hormone ghrelin. Traverso, who is also a gastroenterologist, says that such ‘electroceutical’ devices are being explored as a way to regulate the gut–brain connection. They are potentially less invasive than are procedures such as bariatric surgery and implants that regulate the activity of the digestive system.

rss_4_1790027450.title: China punishes prominent academics exposed by research sleuth
rss_4_1790027450.text:
A social-media sleuth known as Student Geng has released a series of videos highlighting cases of alleged research misconduct.Credit: Tom Houghton/Nature

China’s national funding agency has reprimanded and penalized four senior academics and their colleagues after a sleuth flagged data anomalies in their published papers.

The National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) found violations ranging from data fabrication to data tampering in four papers, according to an announcement from the agency on 28 August.

The academics and their colleagues were banned from applying for funding from the NSFC, either as individuals or members of teams, for between three and seven years. The agency also cancelled funded research projects related to three of the four papers and recovered the money that it had already distributed to them.

Geng Hongwei, the sleuth and video blogger who called out the papers, known online as Student Geng, says that the severity of the punishments is in line with his expectations. He also says that he feels “a little proud” that his efforts, highlighted in a series of viral videos, have led to an official response.

‘Student Geng’ ignites research-integrity scandal in China after calling out senior academics

The penalties were part of a wider crackdown on research misconduct by the NSFC, with 31 research groups and institutes identified in the agency’s statement. Some of the other offences addressed include buying and selling data, plagiarism and misuse of research funds.

Although the NSFC’s statement does not provide the titles of the papers in question, Nature journalists have verified that all four of them were published in Nature or Nature-branded journals. Two were retracted on 29 July and the others now contain editor’s notes acknowledging concerns about their data. Geng said that a key reason that all of the papers he raised concerns about were published in Nature-branded journals is that these journals require researchers to publish their raw data, making his investigations possible.

Nature’s careers and news teams are independent of the journal’s research section and its publisher, Springer Nature. When contacted for comment, Erika Pastrana, vice-president of the Nature research and reviews journals, said that “all papers flagged to us will be investigated”. The journals “will provide updates on papers with editor’s notes once investigations are complete”.

Social-media sleuth

Geng scrutinized the four academics and their papers in videos that went viral in April and May. At that time, all four of them held senior positions at Chinese universities and had received prestigious grants from the NSFC.

The reprimanded academics are Wang Ping, former dean of the School of Life Sciences and Technology at Tongji University in Shanghai; Chen Quan, former dean of the College of Life Sciences at Nankai University in Tianjin; Kuang Dongming, former deputy dean of the School of Life Sciences at Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou; and Su Jiacan, former dean of the Institute of Translational Medicine at Shanghai University. Before the NSFC’s announcement, these academics had already been investigated and disciplined by their universities, including having their deanships removed.

Nature journalists contacted the scientists for comment but had not received any replies at the time of publication.

In the NSFC’s announcement, the agency did not say whether the penalties were a response to Geng’s videos. But Geng says that he filed formal requests with the NSFC for each of the four papers to be investigated, and notes that the agency informed him personally of the results of its investigations (Nature could not independently verify this). Geng’s videos provoked public outcry in China and attracted attention from international media. The videos criticizing the four papers have garnered nearly nine million clicks on Bilibili, a Chinese video-sharing platform.

‘Stamp out paper mills’ — science sleuths on how to fight fake research

The NSFC’s punishments are “very severe”, says Futao Huang, a researcher of higher-education policy at Hiroshima University in Higashihiroshima, Japan.

“For leading researchers, an NSFC funding ban can make it extremely difficult to maintain a laboratory, recruit students and staff or continue major research projects,” he says. “The reputational consequences may be even more damaging.”

For Sun Ping, editor-in-chief of the International Research Collaboration Information Platform, a Beijing-based website that provides information about research-integrity policies and best practice, such punishments aren’t necessarily career-ending for penalized researchers, especially early-career scientists accused of only minor offences. These academics can still participate in research as a team member rather than as a lab leader, he notes.

Geng has called out various other prominent scholars on social media since April, alleging that their papers also included falsified data. Some of those papers now include correction notices, but have not been retracted. It is unclear whether the other scientists called out by Geng will face official investigation by their universities or the NSFC.

rss_5_1790027451.title: AI co-scientists are revolutionizing how research is done
rss_5_1790027451.text:
Biochemist Anna Pertl typed in her question, pressed Enter and left for the night.

The artificial-intelligence system that she had prompted is designed to produce innovative scientific hypotheses. But, unlike a typical chatbot, this AI tool — called Co-Scientist — doesn’t simply generate an answer in a single pass. It launches several autonomous AI systems, known as agents, to search for and synthesize information from papers, evaluate competing explanations, refine and critique hypotheses and iteratively test ideas against published evidence.

Why AI cannot do good science without humans

The process can involve vast quantities of computational power because agents pursue distinct lines of reasoning before converging on workable solutions. And that takes time. Long enough, Pertl jokes, for her to complete a long-distance triathlon, which she has done eight times since she started her PhD at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

On a rainy Tuesday in July, Pertl put the AI system to work on one of cancer’s most complicated problems. She asked Co-Scientist for non-obvious but practical ways of harnessing the biology of molecular droplets known as condensates to shut down MYC, a protein that runs amok in most cancers and has long defied attack attempts.

The request built on years of research by Pertl’s supervisor, Whitehead biologist Richard Young. In 2018, Young and his colleagues found that cells switch on crucial genes by gathering regulatory proteins into condensates that cluster at important genome-control regions called super-enhancers1. They also worked out how cancer cells hijack these super-enhancers to send the gene encoding MYC into overdrive, a strong hint that condensates help to fuel the high expression rate of the protein2.

To Young, the obvious next step is to target the tumour cells’ condensates directly. Dewpoint Therapeutics in Boston, Massachusetts, a company that he co-founded, is now exploring that option. However, because previous attempts to subdue MYC failed, Pertl wanted to see whether AI could come up with a fresh line of attack.

Getting to an idea worth pursuing took some work. Pertl and Whitehead bioengineer Kalon Overholt spent close to an hour going back and forth with Co-Scientist before it understood the question. At first, the AI model assumed that the protein clusters at the centre of the research were meant to be the drug rather than the target. The tool also assumed that the clusters always activated gene expression, when in fact some do the opposite.

Once Pertl and Overholt had corrected these misconceptions, they set the system loose. By the next day, Co-Scientist had combed through more than 700 scientific papers and generated 108 possible strategies. It rejected all but one of the approaches as unworkable. The last strategy turned the laboratory’s thinking on its head.

Rather than dissolving the clusters — the method that Dewpoint is pursuing — the AI tool proposed gluing them together. Using a molecular linking technology called click chemistry, the approach smushes proteins that either activate or repress the MYC gene into one gooey mass, setting off a chain reaction until MYC’s DNA can no longer be read.

Scientists already knew that DNA and the proteins surrounding it could turn from a loose liquid into something firmer, stiffening like gelatin in a refrigerator. But exploiting that transition to shut down a cancer gene was uncharted territory. “It’s extremely conceptually compelling,” says Overholt. “We had certainly never thought about anything like this.”

Trust, but verify

This kind of AI-assisted brainstorming is becoming increasingly common. Researchers have already used Co-Scientist, developed by Google in Mountain View, California, to find a drug combination that kills leukaemia cells in a dish3 and identify a treatment that, in the lab, regenerates liver tissue damaged by disease4.

And Co-Scientist isn’t the only game in town. Frontier AI labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, and start-ups such as FutureHouse5 and Phylo6 (all four based in or around San Francisco, California) are rolling out systems that can tackle tasks once reserved for human scientists, freeing researchers to focus on the most consequential questions and decisions. “We imagine it to be like a collaborator — a partner with you,” says Vivek Natarajan, an AI researcher at Google, who helped to develop Co-Scientist.

Teams of AI agents boost speed of research

That could change not just how scientists work, but also how they are valued. For generations, scientific progress has depended on researchers who could pose difficult questions, devise ways to answer them and make sense of the results. As machines take over more of that work, the scarce resource could end up being human scientific judgement: knowing which questions are worth asking and which lines of enquiry worth pursuing. “The most valuable part now is actually asking the question,” says Ajay Agrawal, an economist at the University of Toronto Rotman School of Management in Canada, who studies AI’s effects on innovation and entrepreneurship.

The goal, says Le Cong, a molecular geneticist at Stanford University in California and scientific co-founder of Phylo, is not to replace researchers but to free them from the routine aspects of discovery. “We’re trying to move humans up the value chain,” he says.

But the adoption of these AI tools also creates a troubling paradox. Researchers might need deeper knowledge than ever to judge whether an AI-generated idea is sound, even as students get fewer opportunities to build that expertise by doing the work themselves. The tools that promise to accelerate discovery could therefore make it harder to train the scientists needed to oversee them.

“Investigators with human skills that understand the full picture are going to be more valuable than ever,” concludes Hector Zenil, a biomedical computing researcher at King’s College London.

For Fyodor Urnov, who studies genome editing at the University of California, Berkeley, and was an early adopter of FutureHouse’s Kosmos platform, the promise of AI research assistants comes with a simple rule: don’t take their pronouncements on faith.

Urnov grew up in Moscow and remembers well a phrase popularized during the 1980s nuclear-arms-control negotiations between the United States and the Soviet Union. “My relationship with [Kosmos] is very much based on that Reagan–Gorbachev proverb,” he says: “Trust, but verify.”

Anna Pertl used Co-Scientist to look for ways to target the cancer-associated protein MYC.Credit: Anna Pertl

A verification step was built into a test of Google’s Co-Scientist by researchers at Imperial College London, who used the platform in 2025 while investigating how bacteria swap snippets of DNA across species7. They had already collected experimental data and formed a theory, but rather than feeding those into the system, they held the unpublished results back and asked the AI tool to work from the publicly available literature and data sets alone. Only after it had produced its theory did they reveal the experimental findings and compare the platform’s work with their own.

Co-Scientist’s theory of what was happening closely matched what the researchers, microbiologists José Penadés and Tiago Costa, had spent years working out: bacterial DNA elements can borrow parts of viruses to spread between distantly related hosts. Thanks to its ability to reason across and connect information from many sources, Co-Scientist reached essentially the same conclusion in about two days7. Had the Imperial researchers used the tool from the start, Costa says, it could have saved them the years of exploratory experiments that they conducted before they hit on the right mechanism.

“If you think about scientific discovery as a 100-metre race,” he says, with an AI assistant “you start this race at, say, metre 30 instead of metre 0”.

AI assistants generally use several agents to attack the same question from different angles. They can break scientific questions into smaller tasks, with agents tackling different pieces in parallel. The Google system — and competing platforms by FutureHouse, Huawei Technologies in Shenzhen, China8, and Sakana AI in Tokyo9 — can explore several possible paths at once, allowing useful connections to emerge from the interplay between agents rather than from a single chain of reasoning.

“You have all these AI agents with different backgrounds to give different perspectives,” says Kyle Swanson, a computer scientist at Stanford who helped to develop Virtual Lab, an early academic AI research-assistant platform10. “It gives you instant access to interdisciplinary experts.”

Importance of good questions

But even a team of AI specialists requires someone to point the tool towards a worthwhile problem and to frame the challenge in such a way that the system can tackle it productively.

For a narrowly defined problem, the goal might be obvious. Perhaps this is why decades-old problems posed by the late Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdős and solved by an AI tool in May proved fertile ground for machine logic. However, in open-ended science, deciding what to ask, and what would count as a meaningful answer, remains a fundamentally human task.

Human scientists trounce the best AI agents on complex tasks

“You have to ask really good questions,” Swanson points out. “If you ask very generic questions, then you’ll probably get very generic answers.”

Not that good questions necessarily require a tightly framed scope. For example, Philine Guckelberger, a molecular geneticist at FutureHouse and Stanford, fed Kosmos a large data set of molecular contacts that help to control which genes are switched on. She then asked the tool to hunt for patterns that a human researcher might overlook.

Kosmos initially stumbled over how the data were labelled, failing to make distinctions that seemed obvious to Guckelberger but had tripped up the tool. In one 30-million-row data set, for instance, it ignored a column in which two types of DNA region were distinguished. After Guckelberger corrected it, the system uncovered an unexpected pattern in cancer cells that she was able to confirm in independent data sets.

“It accelerated this like crazy,” she says.

From start to finish

Another appeal of AI co-scientist platforms is that they can compress the most tedious parts of the research process and take on complex, multistep workflows a scientist would otherwise have to work out by hand.

rss_6_1790027452.title: How do I change labs gracefully during my PhD?
rss_6_1790027452.text:
The problem Dear Nature, I’m a graduate student in biochemistry at a prestigious institution in the United States, and I’ve concluded that I’m in the wrong laboratory. I’m constantly exhausted and my project isn’t one I’m truly passionate about. Our principal investigator (PI), who is also my adviser, is something of a star in their field, so they’re rarely around to provide me with in-depth mentoring. I’ve had to lean heavily on staff scientists and postdocs in the lab for help, but my experiments aren’t working, I feel my progress has stalled and I fear I’m not getting the support I need from my adviser. I’d like to find an adviser who is a better match for my skills and work style, but the process seems fraught with landmines. I’m concerned my present adviser will take my departure personally and might even retaliate. I’m also worried about funding and whether starting over could push my graduation date far off into the future. Changing labs midway through a PhD seems uncommon, but there has to be a way to approach this problem without burning bridges or otherwise hurting my career. How can I leave this situation behind gracefully and transition to a lab that is a better fit for my interests and style of work, while preserving relationships? — Not a bridge burner

The advice

You’ve already taken a healthy first step by identifying one of your key goals: preserving good professional relationships, no matter what path you chart for yourself going forwards. By using skills you already have as a scientist (gathering data, problem-solving and looking for positive ways of resolving to thorny issues), you’re likely to find a way to regroup.

Nature spoke to current and former graduate students, ombudspersons and academic leaders at several major research institutions around the world, and a career counsellor for PhD students, about navigating your situation and making informed decisions as to whether and how to change labs during your training years.

Define your goals

Jennifer Polk, a career counsellor based in Toronto, Canada, who advises PhD students who wish to craft careers outside of academia, says that you should “give yourself the grace that you need” to define, and perhaps redefine, your goals. What you thought you wanted at the beginning of your PhD programme could change as the reality of the day-to-day grind of lab research sets in. “The clearer you are about what you want, the better,” Polk says.

The office of the ombudsperson at your institution could be a good place to start an informal, confidential conversation around a perceived mismatch with your adviser. Many other institutions, both in the United States and internationally, have a similar person in place to resolve conflicts. Katrin Jordan, head of the research directorate at the Dresden University of Technology in Germany, says that German universities provide graduate students with “persons of trust”, who function as a source of support. “These advisers are available for early-career researchers,” Jordan says. “When a student says, ‘OK, I’m not happy’, we can try to mediate and to facilitate a switch if possible.” Other places to look for support might include trusted members of your dissertation committee, or the office of your institution’s director of graduate instruction.

Craft your approach

There are a few options open to you. If the issue is a purely scientific one (for example, your research interests have changed), you might be able to transfer to a different lab while ensuring that your current supervisor remains on your dissertation committee. Alternatively, you could ask for a co-supervisor if you don’t already have one, who could help you to shift the focus of your project or provide extra support.

“We often talk to people proactively about having more than one mentor,” whether acting formally or informally, says Ellen Goldstein, director of the Office of the Ombuds at the University of California, San Francisco. “It's good, practically, because you learn different styles of leadership. You learn about different kinds of science. You learn about different perspectives.”

Another approach, especially if you’ve completed most of your graduate work or if it is not possible to secure funding to change labs, is to shorten your time to graduation. One former graduate student whose mentor won a Nobel prize described a highly competitive work culture in her lab that allowed little time for anything except research. “I don’t have a competitive bone in my body,” she told Nature. “I was deep into my project, and I approached [my mentor] with some trepidation about leaving,” she said. “But [they] heard me and agreed that we would figure out what body of work I needed to do to complete my degree.”

Challenges can arise when the reason for wanting to make a change involves interpersonal friction. It’s understandable that you are concerned about retaliation or severing relationships. Shirley Nakata, the ombudsperson for students at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada, emphasizes that although advisers, ombudspersons and members of your dissertation committee can help to guide you, it’s important to be realistic about the balance of power in relationships with advisers. “You’re not going to change the behaviour of a star PI,” she counsels. That could require treading lightly when navigating difficult interpersonal issues.

Hold key conversations

Communicate clearly with your PI, centring conversations around mutually beneficial goals. You might also wish to identify potential new advisers and discreetly discuss with them the possibility of a move before reaching out to your current adviser. Your new mentor will need adequate funding if your existing funding cannot be transferred, and this could limit your ability to move between labs. You will also need to discuss timing: it could take longer to graduate if your research is not transferable to the new lab, but acquiring the experience you’re actually looking for in your graduate studies might be worth the trade-off.

When speaking to your current adviser, “you want to do it thoughtfully and honestly”, Polk says. Approach the conversation with curiosity and open-mindedness.

rss_7_1790027453.title: 'Epigenetic' editing is here: gene-tagging technique banishes hepatitis B virus
rss_7_1790027453.text:
A wave of epigenetic therapies is offering hope as ways to cure chronic hepatitis B — a lingering liver infection that is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV) and affects more than 250 million people around the world. Currently available drugs often fail to eradicate the virus from the body.

Gene-editing therapies — which make cuts to the DNA strands — have been explored but for hepatitis B, they can increase cancer risks. Researchers are turning instead to epigenetic editing, which modifies markers attached to the DNA to alter how genes are turned on and off.

Scientists working at the biotechnology firm nChroma Bio in Boston, Massachusetts, and at institutes in Milan, Italy, have now placed chemical tags onto the HBV genome to shut down its gene activity and prevent it from producing viral particles. They achieved promising results in experiments on human liver cells and in mice, and the therapy generated only minimal and temporary side effects when tested in monkeys. The study was published in Nature Biomedical Engineering on 21 September1.

‘Epigenetic’ editing cuts cholesterol in mice

The efficacy of a single injection was “quite impressive”. This “is really where we need to go to end up being able to address this pandemic of HBV around the world”, says John Tavis, a molecular virologist at Saint Louis University in Missouri.

The preclinical findings “supported clinical advancement of this approach”, says study co-author Angelo Lombardo, a molecular biologist at the San Raffaele Telethon Institute for Gene Therapy in Milan, Italy. nChroma Bio has now launched a clinical trial to test multiple doses of the treatment in Hong Kong and New Zealand. The first participant received the therapy, through an intravenous infusion, in January.

The trial in humans is “a huge step” and “a realization of many, many years of work”, adds Lombardo, who co-founded nChroma Bio but does not have an official role at the firm. nChroma Bio declined Nature’s request to comment on the study.

Targeting hidden copies

HBV infections can turn into life-long challenges because the virus has ways to remain in the body and trick the immune system into not fighting against it. One of these is making free-ranging mini-chromosomes that can hide inside liver cells for a very long time.

These twists of viral DNA form “a genomic archive of the virus”, which help it to replicate when people stop taking anti-HBV drugs and lead to a severe rebound of the disease, explains virologist and clinical hepatologist Fabien Zoulim at the University of Lyon in France. Less than 10% of people who are treated for HBV for at least 10 years can cease their daily medications without such risk, Zoulim adds.

HBV can also stitch pieces of its genome into its host’s DNA and generate proteins that alter the immune response against it. The integration of viral DNA causes molecular changes in liver cells that can lead to cancer, Zoulim says.

nChroma’s therapy — named CRMA-1001 — contains a version of CRISPR’s Cas9 enzyme that lacks its normal enzymatic cutting activity. It also features RNA strands that lead the enzyme to its specific target in the HBV genome.

Encapsulated in a lipid nanoparticle, the therapy pulls a double duty to silence both free-ranging and integrated HBV DNAs by tagging them with methyl groups.

rss_10_1790027458.title: Daily briefing: How to turn a paper into an AI agent
rss_10_1790027458.text:
A new tool is designed to help researchers interact with published papers. Plus, promising news for an RNA-based treatment for ALS and how psychoactive drugs might have shaped pre-Incan culture.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Stephen Hawking worked on the black-hole information paradox throughout his life.Credit: Santi Visalli/Getty

An RNA therapy for rare forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has shown promising results in the first person to receive it. He experienced improved symptoms and continued to work as a physician a year after starting treatment. Antisense oligonucleotide therapy uses short strands of genetic material to target RNA produced by a faulty gene called CHCHD10. Roughly 5–10% of people with ALS have a known genetic mutation, and antisense oligonucleotide therapies could someday benefit them and others with neurodegenerative diseases caused by rare mutations.

Nature | 7 min read

Reference: Med paper

Chinese firms subject to sanctions by the US government seemed to produce more science-related patents and publish more papers than did unsanctioned companies. It’s not certain that being placed on the US ‘Entity List’ actually caused an increase in innovation, but the findings might be a sign of unintended consequences of such restrictions. “Whether or not one supports technology controls, it is important to recognize that they can come with costs,” says political economist Dinsha Mistree.

Nature | 7 min read

Reference: Science paper

Features & opinion

Chavín de Huántar, a 3,000-year-old temple complex high in the Peruvian Andes, has long been thought to be a centre for rituals amplified by the use of psychoactive drugs. Now advances that make it possible to detect the faintest traces of chemical and biological substances — and a research environment that is increasingly open to the topic of hallucinogens and other drugs — are adding to the evidence of what happened there.

Science | 20 min read

The latest short story for Nature’s Futures series asks: as nature declines, how can we grieve for a world we have never known? It is environmental researcher Hannah Cocks’s first published creative writing piece. “I hope the first of many,” she writes. “I would like to write to remind us that we are part of nature and always have been.”

Nature | 6 min read

Andrew Robinson’s pick of the top five science books to read this week includes an engaging study of the relationship between astrology and science, a celebration of polio vaccine pioneer Albert Sabin and a vision of the social world that exists around, outside and in opposition to money.

Nature | 4 min read

In this week’s Nature Podcast, hosts Benjamin Thompson and Nick Petrić Howe speak to researchers about a new study in which human brain organoids were transplanted into mice genetically engineered to lack most of their cerebral cortex.

Nature Podcast | 27 min listen

rss_11_1790027459.title: Europe pushes for space independence amid geopolitical rifts
rss_11_1790027459.text:
The uncrewed Spectrum launch vehicle is the first commercial rocket to be sent into orbit from continental Europe.Credit: Isar Aerospace

Momentum is growing for Europe to develop its own sovereign space capabilities, including satellite launches and human spaceflight, and reduce its dependence on the United States as divisions grow across the Atlantic.

“Our security on Earth increasingly depends on our security in space,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said at the inaugural International Space Summit in Paris, France on 10 September. “Europe must act together, invest at scale, and turn our market into a competitive advantage.”

Europe currently relies on NASA and companies such as SpaceX in Brownsville, Texas, to launch some of its astronauts and satellites to space. SpaceX’s Starlink network of broadband satellites in low-Earth orbit is now the leading provider of Internet from space around the world. And commercial European space activity has lagged behind that of the United States. Of the global US$13.5 billion invested in space companies last year, only 12% went to European companies, compared with 68% for US organizations.

But change is in the air. The European Space Agency (ESA), the European Union, national governments and private companies are gearing up to give Europe greater autonomy in space than it has had previously.

Space-summit snub

The latest developments come after the White House was reported to have discouraged US space companies such as SpaceX and Blue Origin from attending the Paris summit, according to reporting from Politico and others. During the meeting, president of France Emmanuel Macron spoke of his desire for Europe to develop the ability to achieve human spaceflight independently. “Europe must fly with its own crews,” he said.

Eva Berneke, previously the chief executive of the French satellite company Eutelsat, told Nature that the last-minute cancellation by “the big Americans” was a “wake-up call” for Europe to push for greater sovereignty. “Europe needs to step up,” she says, after previous tensions with the US had raised alarms.

US agencies have also eased on some collaborations. For example, last week, NASA said that it would no longer supply an instrument for a European Space Agency mission to Venus called Envision, set to launch in 2031.

Lift-off efforts

One of the key areas that Europe needs to strengthen to become more independent is its launch capabilities. The Ariane and Vega series of rockets, which take off from a spaceport in French Guiana, South America, are European but the region lacks a well-developed private rocket industry similar to those in the United States and, in the past few years, China.

On 5 September, the German commercial rocket company Isar Aerospace launched the first orbital rocket to take off from European soil from the Andøya spaceport in Norway. And several European companies are developing reusable rockets and heavy-lift launchers, crucial for sending satellites into space frequently.

A spaceport in Andøya, Norway, will increase Europe’s spacecraft launch capacity. Credit: Isar Aerospace

Europe’s launch industry is unlikely to grow to rival that of the United States and China, says Bleddyn Bowen, an astropolitics researcher at Durham University, UK, but Europe can make sure that it “has enough essential infrastructure in space” with its own rockets.

A Starlink competitor called IRIS2, a constellation of 348 satellites set to begin launching in 2029, is also being developed by the European Union. It will supply civilians, businesses, emergency services and the military with Internet from space — providing Europe with a way to stay online without relying on SpaceX.

“IRIS2 has been talked about for many, many years,” says Bowen. “Now, things are actually getting built.”

Investment on the rise

Defence spending on space technology has increased in European nations, too. Most notably, Germany plans to invest €35 billion (around $40 billion) into spy satellites, space planes and other military equipment by 2030.

Commercial space companies in Europe, meanwhile, have seen some sizeable investments this year. On 8 September, The Exploration Company in Gauting, Germany, announced that it had secured $450 million in funding — one of the largest amounts raised in European space history — to build a spacecraft called Nyx to launch cargo and, eventually, humans.
